known_research_boundaries: Set Paris 1783, using a composite modest household and a composite affluent urban household. Avoid substituting Versailles for every prosperous city house. Main twist: a cabbage can be an elaborate meat-garnish recipe, and access to fuel/cooks/shop ovens changes what reaches a plate. Mercier is a vivid contemporary critic, not a neutral dataset. His own ordinary-meal account (soup, boiled beef, Sunday mutton) refutes a blanket meatless-poor narrative. His sausage anecdote supports a small purchase, not an invented complete daily ration. Read his surrounding social polemic to avoid adopting stereotypes or fantastical statistical certainty. Menon's1755 Paris cookbook independently supports exact preparation sequences and planned reuse of roast poultry, challenging the idea that all rich leftovers were waste. It is a prescription, so the narrator explicitly chooses a period recipe for the reconstruction. No unverified causal claim linking one menu directly to revolution. Food and labour remain the story; methodological qualifications are concise. No modern dollar conversions or precise household food budget. Bibliographic date verified by Wellcome. Cairn's2004 butcher-hygiene study was inaccessible except snippets and is not used.
